engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Pin
chess.body: A pin prevents a piece from moving because moving it would expose a more valuable piece behind it. Absolute pin = pinned to the king (piece cannot move legally). Relative pin = pinned to queen/rook (can move but it's a blunder). Identify pins in every position. Then exploit them.

wisdom.title: Stoic Parenting
wisdom.body: Marcus Aurelius raised children while running an empire. His journal shows he constantly asked: am I reacting or responding? Reacting is automatic. Responding is chosen. The next time your baby cries at 2am, ask yourself: how do I want to respond to this? You always have a choice in the gap between stimulus and response.

book.author: Angela Duckworth
book.chapter: Passion and Perseverance: The Formula That Beats Talent
book.lesson: Duckworth's research across West Point cadets, Scripps spelling bee champions, and sales teams found that the most important predictor of success was not talent, IQ, or physical fitness. It was grit — the combination of passion for a long-term goal and the perseverance to pursue it despite obstacles and setbacks. Grit predicts success better than talent in almost every domain. The most talented people often lack grit because things have come too easily — they've never had to develop the capacity to push through failure. The grittier person with modest talent consistently outperforms the talented person who quits.
book.key_quote: Talent × effort = skill. Skill × effort = achievement. Effort counts twice.
book.action: Identify one long-term goal you've been inconsistent about. What would it look like to commit to it with grit — showing up daily regardless of motivation?
crux: Grit = passion + perseverance for long-term goals. It predicts achievement better than talent.
Talent × effort = skill. Skill × effort = achievement. Effort counts twice.
Our preference for 'naturals' hides how much of performance is accumulated work.
Grit is measurable, and it predicts West Point completion, sales retention, and spelling-bee results.
Interest comes before passion. Passion is developed by deliberate cultivation, not found.
Deliberate practice: a stretch goal, full concentration, immediate feedback, repetition on weakness.
Purpose — the belief that the work matters to others — is what sustains effort past year three.
Hope here is not optimism. It is the belief that your own effort changes the outcome.
Goal hierarchy: one top-level goal, mid-level goals as means, low-level as tasks. Drop anything that doesn't serve the top.
Gritty people quit constantly — at the low level. Never at the top.
Grit grows with age and can be trained deliberately.
Hard Thing Rule: everyone does something hard, you may quit only at a natural end point, and you pick the hard thing yourself.
Gritty cultures build gritty individuals. Environment does much of the work.
learnings: Consistency over years beats intensity over weeks, and it is less glamorous.
Passion is cultivated, so 'find your passion' is bad advice.
Deliberate practice is uncomfortable by design. Comfortable practice is repetition.
Purpose is what keeps effort going when interest dips.
examples: West Point's Beast Barracks: the Grit Scale predicted who stayed better than the Whole Candidate Score.
Spelling-bee finalists were separated by hours of solitary deliberate practice, not by verbal IQ.
Julia Child was 37 and had no cooking credentials when she started. Mastery came from sustained years, not aptitude.
adapt: Top-level goal: financial independence with the family in one place. Everything else is a means and can be dropped.
Hard Thing Rule for the household — one hard voluntary thing each, quit only at a season's end.
Deliberate practice on modelling: pick the weakest area, get feedback, repeat. Not more of what already works.
Mid-2026 is 10 months. Grit is what makes month 7 look the same as month 1.

father.title: Wait out the frustration noise
father.do: When she grumbles at a task, wait. Only step in if it escalates to genuine distress.
father.why: There is a difference between frustration and distress, and learning to tell them apart is a skill you build now. Frustration tolerated becomes persistence; frustration always rescued becomes helplessness.

father.title: Check the floor at her eye level
father.do: Lie on the floor and look across the room from her height. Remove what you find.
father.why: Mobility arrives suddenly. Anything reachable at that height will be in her mouth within days of her crawling, and you will not get advance notice.

speaking.title: Answer, then stop
speaking.drill: Ask yourself an interview question, answer it, and physically close your mouth. Count three seconds before adding anything.
speaking.why: Over-explaining after a complete answer is the most common interview mistake at senior level. The silence is theirs to fill.

interview_tech.q: What is the difference between EBITDA and free cash flow, and which do you manage to?
interview_tech.a: EBITDA ignores working capital movements, capex, tax and interest. A retailer can grow EBITDA while burning cash by stuffing stores with inventory and opening capital-hungry sites. Free cash flow = EBITDA − capex − change in working capital − tax − interest. Manage the business to free cash flow; report EBITDA because that is what lenders and multiples use. Where they diverge for more than two quarters, something structural is wrong.

interview_tech.q: What breaks first when a retailer scales from 60 to 200 stores?
interview_tech.a: Not the finance system — the master data and the operating cadence. Specifically: SKU and price master governance, because inconsistent data makes every report wrong; the supply chain's ability to replenish without central stock-outs; and the management reporting rhythm, because a weekly review that works for 60 stores becomes noise at 200 without exception-based reporting. Finance's job is to install store-level P&L discipline and exception thresholds before the growth, not after.

interview_soft.q: What would your last manager say is your weakness?
interview_soft.a: Name a real one with a boundary. The pattern that works: a genuine weakness, evidence you know its cost, and the specific mechanism you use to contain it. 'I go too deep into detail before surfacing a view — it has cost me time on low-stakes analysis. I now set a decision deadline before starting and present at that point regardless of how complete it feels.' Avoid perfectionism, avoid anything that would disqualify you for the role itself.

interview_soft.q: What is the hardest decision you have made in your career?
interview_soft.a: Hard means genuinely two-sided, not merely unpleasant. Redundancies, closing a site, overruling someone you respected, or choosing between two people for one role. Structure: the trade-off, the information you had and did not have, how you decided, what it cost, and what you would do differently. Interviewers discount any answer where the right choice was obvious in hindsight — say what made it genuinely close.

cfo_field.q: Explain a variance in one sentence or you do not understand it yet.
cfo_field.a: 'Margin is down 180bps: 120 from promotional depth in electronics, 40 from freight, 20 mix.' That is a CFO answer. A table of forty lines is a controller answer. The discipline is to decompose until the drivers are additive and then name the largest two. If you cannot make the bridge add up, you have a data problem, not a communication problem.

cfo_field.q: Working capital is where a retail CFO is actually judged.
cfo_field.a: EBITDA gets the headline; the cash conversion cycle gets the board's attention. DIO + DSO − DPO. Retail is inventory-heavy and often near-zero DSO, so the fight is DIO against DPO. Cutting DIO from 95 to 80 days on AED 400M COGS releases roughly AED 16.4M of cash — permanently, without selling a single extra unit. That is a bigger number than most cost programmes deliver, and it does not need a headcount conversation.

lichess_games.standout: 3 blunders in one game. The result is noise; the error count is the signal.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: avoid 6.Qh5? and 9.Bc4?; instead develop knights, castle by move 12, and keep pawn structure solid (e.g., play … c3, d4). This prevents quick attacks and reduces check‑mate threats.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your 0‑0‑2 record shows a complete collapse against even modest opposition—your opening repertoire is either nonexistent or fundamentally unsound, and you never transition into a playable middlegame. Stop relying on “trendy” lines; adopt a rock‑solid, low‑theory system (e.g., Caro‑Kann for Black, London System for White) and drill the critical pawn structures and typical tactical motifs until they become automatic. Spend the next 10 hours reviewing every loss move‑by‑move, annotate every mistake, and then play 30 blitz games focusing solely on executing the first ten moves flawlessly before moving on to deeper analysis.
